decision: The one number that says the site worked
options: Share of regulars' usual loaves reserved ahead and collected
Total online orders per week
Number of sourdough sellouts at walk-in
recommendation: Share of regulars' usual loaves reserved ahead and collected
reason: It measures the real promise, that regulars get their loaf before it sells out, rather than raw order volume.
question: What would tell you a regular's morning has genuinely got easier because of this site?

decision: What we measure at 'Reserve your usual'
options: Count one-tap usual reservations per returning customer per week
Count clicks on the reserve button
Count repeat reservations only after 4 weeks
recommendation: Count one-tap usual reservations per returning customer per week
reason: It shows whether reserving the usual is effortless and repeated, which is what regulars come back for.
question: How often do you picture a regular reserving the same loaf, and what makes that habit stick?

label: Reserve your usual
reason: It shows whether reserving the usual is effortless and repeated, which is what regulars come back for.
decision: What we measure at 'Reserve your usual'
What we measure at 'Pick up bread'
options: Count orders marked collected versus no-show per day
Ask customers to confirm pickup
Don't track pickup
recommendation: Count orders marked collected versus no-show per day
reason: Collected versus no-show tells the baker if reserved loaves are wasted and whether the guarantee holds.

decision: What we keep about a customer's orders and for how long
options: Keep name, contact and usual loaf; delete after 12 months of inactivity
Keep all order history indefinitely
Keep only the current order, nothing remembered
recommendation: Keep name, contact and usual loaf; delete after 12 months of inactivity
reason: Remembering the usual is needed to feel known, while limiting retention keeps personal data to what a decision uses.

note: Data sheet: one measure per journey step, centred on regulars getting their usual loaf, with a single whole-page success number.

decision: Pay online at ordering, or pay at the counter on pickup
options: Pay at the counter on pickup
Pay online when ordering
Let the customer choose either
recommendation: Pay at the counter on pickup
reason: Regulars already pay in the shop, so reserving stays a one-tap habit and the bakery avoids card fees and refund handling at the start.
question: What makes a regular trust that their loaf will be waiting, even before they've paid?

decision: What happens to a reserved loaf that is never collected
options: Hold until a set time, then release it to others
Charge for no-shows after repeated misses
Hold all day with no consequence
recommendation: Hold until a set time, then release it to others
reason: A guaranteed loaf only works if unclaimed bread goes back on sale, and a hold-then-release rule costs customers nothing.
question: When a regular doesn't show up, how long should their loaf wait for them?

decision: Whether prices are the shop's normal prices or carry any online surcharge or discount
options: Same price as in the shop
Small discount for pre-ordering
Small fee for reserving
recommendation: Same price as in the shop
reason: Regulars expect to be treated like neighbours, and the owner sets the real prices, so the site just mirrors the shop.

decision: Whether regulars can set a repeating standing order for their usual loaf
options: Repeat reservation they can skip any day
One-off reservations only at first
Paid weekly subscription
recommendation: Repeat reservation they can skip any day
reason: Sourdough regulars want certainty each morning, and a repeat with easy skipping delivers it without prepayment or a subscription.
question: How often does a regular want the same loaf waiting, and how do they change their mind?

label: Reserve your usual
reason: Sourdough regulars want certainty each morning, and a repeat with easy skipping delivers it without prepayment or a subscription.
decision: Whether regulars can set a repeating standing order for their usual loaf

note: Pricing and payment decisions for a bakery pre-order site, centred on guaranteeing regulars their loaf.

decision: What happens when two people reserve the last sourdough
options: First confirmed order wins; the other sees sold out and alternatives
Hold loaf in cart for 10 minutes
Allow oversell and let baker sort it out
recommendation: First confirmed order wins; the other sees sold out and alternatives
reason: A guaranteed loaf is the whole promise, so stock is checked and decremented at the moment of confirming, never oversold.
question: What should happen for a regular when the sourdough runs out before they order?

decision: Whether the page remembers regulars on this device and offers a one-tap usual
options: Remember name, contact and last order on this device, no account
Require an account with login
Remember nothing
recommendation: Remember name, contact and last order on this device, no account
reason: It makes reordering effortless without passwords, and is simple, proven browser storage.
question: How should a regular's usual loaf get reserved without them having to ask?

label: Reserve your usual
reason: It makes reordering effortless without passwords, and is simple, proven browser storage.
decision: Whether the page remembers regulars on this device and offers a one-tap usual
Whether customers pay online or pay at pickup
options: Pay at pickup, order is a reservation
Pay online by card at checkout
Both, customer chooses
recommendation: Pay at pickup, order is a reservation
reason: It avoids handling money and refunds for a small bakery, and regulars already pay at the counter.

decision: How the baker sees orders and what happens if confirmation or storage fails
options: Orders stored in one database, baker gets a daily list page plus email, customer sees on-screen confirmation
Orders emailed only to baker
Text message confirmation to customer too
recommendation: Orders stored in one database, baker gets a daily list page plus email, customer sees on-screen confirmation
reason: One stored source of truth means a failed email never loses an order, and the page shows a clear retry message if saving fails.

note: Engineering decisions for the bakery pre-order page: sold-out handling, remembering regulars, payment, and failure fallback.

decision: What ordering should feel like: remembered and one-tap, or guided step by step
options: Remembered and quick: usual loaf pre-filled, one confirm
Guided and reassuring: every step shown
Remembered for regulars, guided for new visitors
recommendation: Remembered for regulars, guided for new visitors
reason: Her principle says never ask for what we could remember, so the grey wireframes lead with a pre-filled usual and keep the full path as a short fallback (one filled button marks the main action).
question: What does a regular feel when the baker already knows their order the moment they walk in?

decision: What leads the first screen: the regular's usual loaf or the full bread list
options: Reserve your usual as the lead, browse below
Browse breads first, usual as a small link
Same screen for everyone
recommendation: Reserve your usual as the lead, browse below
reason: One filled button marks the main action, and for the morning regulars that action is reserving the usual sourdough, so it sits above browsing in the hierarchy.
question: When a regular opens the site at 6am, what is the one thing they want done?

label: Reserve your usual
reason: One filled button marks the main action, and for the morning regulars that action is reserving the usual sourdough, so it sits above browsing in the hierarchy.
decision: What leads the first screen: the regular's usual loaf or the full bread list
What a sold-out or cut-off state shows for sourdough
options: Say it is gone and offer the next pickup day
Hide sold-out loaves
Show a waitlist
recommendation: Say it is gone and offer the next pickup day
reason: The promise is certainty, so the sold-out state must be plain, honest and give a next step in live text rather than hiding the loaf.
question: What should a regular be told when their sourdough is already spoken for?

decision: Which single accent colour carries the page on warm neutral paper
options: Warm wheat or crust brown
Deep green
Terracotta
recommendation: Warm wheat or crust brown
reason: The interface stays 90 to 95% neutral with one accent, and a crust brown feels familiar and local without using violet or gradients; text must keep 7:1 contrast.

note: Sketched the ordering flow for morning regulars: how it feels, what leads the first screen, how the sold-out state reads, and the accent.

decision: Whether the first version is built for daily morning regulars only
options: Regulars only
Regulars first, occasional buyers can browse
Everyone equally
recommendation: Regulars first, occasional buyers can browse
reason: Her belief and what we know point to regulars who hate missing sourdough, and we'd learn first how many such regulars there are and what time they arrive.
question: Who is the customer you picture standing at the counter when the sourdough is already gone?

decision: How a regular reserves their usual loaf
options: One tap on a remembered usual, repeating daily
Pick loaves each time from the list
Standing weekly order set once
recommendation: One tap on a remembered usual, repeating daily
reason: Her principle is never to ask for what we could remember, and we'd learn first how steady regulars' routines really are.
question: How predictable is a regular's order from one morning to the next?

label: Reserve your usual
reason: Her principle is never to ask for what we could remember, and we'd learn first how steady regulars' routines really are.
decision: How a regular reserves their usual loaf
What promise customers get that their loaf will be waiting
options: Guaranteed loaf once reserved
Reserved until a set time, then released
Best effort, no promise
recommendation: Guaranteed loaf once reserved
reason: Certainty is what regulars come back for, but it is a promise made to customers, and we'd learn first what the baker can reliably commit to.
question: What would make a regular trust that their loaf will really be there?

decision: Whether advance orders are used to tell the baker how many loaves to bake
options: Baker sees a daily count of orders per bread
Baker sees orders only as a list
No planning view in version one
recommendation: Baker sees a daily count of orders per bread
reason: A 2025 small-bakery study (not yet opened by us, so check the link) says bread waste is common and guessing how many to bake contributes, and knowing orders ahead fixes that guess.

options: One-tap 'your usual' for returning regulars, full browse for new people
Same browse-and-pick flow for everyone
Standing daily order that repeats automatically

decision: Whether regulars get a one-tap repeat of their usual loaf, or everyone goes through the same browse-and-pick flow
What the customer sees and can do when sourdough is already reserved or sold out for the day
options: Show it as sold out and offer the next pickup day or a similar loaf
Let people order anyway and the baker sorts it out
Hold a set number of loaves back for regulars only
recommendation: Hold a set number of loaves back for regulars only
reason: The core promise is that regulars get their loaf before it sells out, so some stock must be protected for them rather than first-come.
question: If there are only a few sourdough loaves left, who should get them: regulars or whoever orders first?

decision: How far ahead and by what cutoff customers can choose a pickup day, and what happens if they cancel or change late
options: Next morning and up to 7 days ahead, change or cancel until the evening before
Same-day orders allowed until a morning cutoff
Fixed pickup day only, no changes
recommendation: Next morning and up to 7 days ahead, change or cancel until the evening before
reason: The baker needs the evening before to bake the right amount, and regulars need a simple way to skip a day without calling.
question: When do your regulars know they'll want bread, and how often do their plans change at the last minute?

decision: Whether customers pay online or just reserve and pay at pickup
options: Reserve now, pay at the counter when collecting
Pay online at checkout
Let the customer choose either
recommendation: Reserve now, pay at the counter when collecting
reason: It is the smallest version that works end to end for people who already come in, and it avoids payment setup and refunds for a small bakery.
